title: How the Flexner Report Changed Medicine
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explain the Flexner Report (1910), the Carnegie Foundation bulletin written by Abraham Flexner that reshaped American and Canadian medical education along the Johns Hopkins/German research model. They cover pre-Flexner medicine (proprietary diploma-mill schools, two-year programs), the AMA's role and anti-homeopathy history, Flexner's school-by-school evaluations, the closure of most schools (including five of seven Black medical schools and alternative medicine programs), its sexism and racism, philanthropy (Rockefeller Foundation), and long-term critiques regarding humanism in medicine, psychiatry, and underrepresentation of Black doctors. The episode ends with listener mail from Kyle about the show's purpose.
topics: medicine as a trade vs profession

segments.title: Show open
segments.summary: Network intro before the hosts begin.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Flexner Report, a listener suggestion, and frame it as a report that reshaped US medicine while also suppressing homeopathy and containing racist and sexist views.

segments.title: Pre-Flexner American medicine
segments.summary: Describes US medical schools around 1850 (52 schools, two-year programs, underfunded, diploma mills), the post-Civil War push for reform, and Johns Hopkins' 1893 opening that set a German-influenced model with degree requirements, full-time faculty, and four-year hands-on study.

segments.title: AMA, homeopathy, and the Carnegie push
segments.summary: The AMA, founded 1847, opposed homeopathy and used a consultation clause; the Carnegie Foundation was approached to produce a report favoring the Johns Hopkins model, and Abraham Flexner was chosen as an outsider.

segments.title: Abraham Flexner's background and European report
segments.summary: Flexner's background as an educator and author of The American College; Henry Pritchett's endorsement; Flexner's later European report praising the German system and including anti-Semitic passages; Welch's Germany-inspired Johns Hopkins model.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Playful German-word banter during a break.

segments.title: Off-topic banter
segments.summary: Hosts continue light banter about German words and a Frankenstein film.

segments.title: Flexner's survey of 155 schools
segments.summary: Flexner visited 155 medical schools (148 US, 7 Canada) over about eighteen months, evaluating finances, facilities, admissions, and teaching against Johns Hopkins, sorting each school into keep, improve, or close.

segments.title: Harsh critiques of schools
segments.summary: Examples of Flexner's rankings including Iowa State's medical school, his scornful language about osteopathic schools and admissions, and his view that underfunded schools should close.

segments.title: Recommended closures and proprietary schools
segments.summary: Flexner recommended cutting schools from 155 to 31; proprietary schools were all targeted; medical schools should be publicly funded and tied to universities.

segments.title: Alternative medicine and Black medical schools
segments.summary: Alternative medical systems were shut down; five of seven Black medical schools were recommended for closure; Howard University and Meharry were spared; Chapter Fourteen's racist framing of Black medical education.

segments.title: Sexism, ideal education, and philanthropy
segments.summary: Flexner's views against women doctors; the rigorous model's costs excluded poorer candidates; full-time faculty requirement; foundations including Rockefeller funded the reforms.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the second half.

segments.title: Aftermath: school closures and Black physician shortage
segments.summary: Within five years over fifty US schools closed; by twenty years only 76 of 148 remained; estimates of lost Black doctors; Black patients' preference for Black doctors; links to Tuskegee and mistrust.

segments.title: Humanism lost and academic-clinical split
segments.summary: Critics argue the report's science focus made patients into diagnostic cases; separation of academic and practicing physicians; end-of-life care satisfaction.

segments.title: Alternative medicine, homeopathy, and psychiatry
segments.summary: Discussion of lost mental health approaches (meditation, nutrition, lifestyle) and the neurochemical model of mental illness; a resurgence of lifestyle-based approaches in psychiatry.

segments.title: Overall assessment
segments.summary: Hosts weigh the report's positives (lives saved, lifespans extended) against its harms, arguing that drastic change was needed.

segments.title: Closing and reading suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts thank Emily for the suggestion and recommend reading the report.
